prompt: Order the plans Catalyst produces, first to last.
hint: Names are checked before anything is rewritten.

prompt: A query names a column `kinde` that does not exist. When does it fail?
hint: Which step looks names up in the schema?

choices.text: At analysis, before any data is read
choices.why: Right. Names are checked against the schema there.

choices.text: At the optimisation step
choices.why: Optimisation only rewrites a plan that is already valid.

choices.text: Never; the column is filled with nulls
choices.why: A missing column is an error, not nulls.

choices.text: When the first task reaches a row without that column
choices.why: It never gets that far; analysis refuses it.

prompt: Why does Catalyst do nothing for an RDD `filter(lambda ...)`?
hint: What can it see of a lambda?

choices.text: Catalyst only runs on SQL strings
choices.why: DataFrames go through it too.

choices.text: RDDs are planned by a different optimiser that is off by default
choices.why: There is no optimiser for RDDs at all.

choices.text: RDDs only exist on the driver
choices.why: They are distributed, like DataFrames.

choices.text: Spark sees a function it must run as it is
choices.why: Right. Catalyst works on expressions it can read.

prompt: In the optimised plan, where did the filter on `kind` go, and why?
hint: Compare it with the parsed plan.

choices.text: Nowhere; plans never change the program's order
choices.why: Changing it is what the optimiser is for.

choices.text: Above the sort, so the sort runs first
choices.why: It moved towards the data, not away.

choices.text: Into the books' side of the join
choices.why: `kind` is a column of the clicks.

choices.text: Below the join, onto the clicks
choices.why: Right. Filtering before joining shrinks the join's input.

prompt: What does the number after `#` in `book_id#4` tell Catalyst?

choices.text: Which `book_id` it is
choices.why: Right. `book_id#4` and `book_id#7` are the two sides of the join.

choices.text: How many rows have that value
choices.why: No data has been read when plans are made.

choices.text: The column's position in the file
choices.why: It is an id given by Catalyst, not a position.

choices.text: The partition it lives in
choices.why: Partitions are about rows, not columns.

prompt: The physical plan joined the clicks to the books with a ___HashJoin, copying the books to every task.
What is every `Exchange` node in a physical plan?

choices.text: A shuffle
choices.why: Right, and the boundary of a stage.

choices.text: A file being read
choices.why: That is a `Scan`.

choices.text: A write to HDFS
choices.why: Shuffle files go to local disk.

choices.text: A join
choices.why: Joins have their own nodes; an exchange may feed one.

prompt: Why are there two `HashAggregate` nodes around the first `Exchange`?

choices.text: One counts purchases, the other counts books
choices.why: Both count the same thing, in two halves.

choices.text: The second one checks the first
choices.why: It adds the partial counts, it does not check them.

choices.text: Counting in two halves, around a shuffle
choices.why: Right. Each task sends a few counts instead of every row.

choices.text: AQE added a duplicate
choices.why: Both are in the initial plan.

prompt: The sort's `Exchange` uses `rangepartitioning`, not `hashpartitioning`. Why?
hint: Lesson 4: what does a globally sorted output need?

choices.text: There are only ten categories
choices.why: The count of keys does not decide the partitioner.

choices.text: Range partitioning is always faster
choices.why: It costs a sampling pass; it is chosen for order.

choices.text: The counts are numbers and cannot be hashed
choices.why: Numbers hash fine.

choices.text: Each task must hold a range of values
choices.why: Right. Hashing would scatter neighbours across tasks.

prompt: The formatted plan has two `Exchange` nodes and one `BroadcastExchange`. How many shuffles does the query do?
hint: A broadcast is not a shuffle.

prompt: `size of files read` was 388.8 MiB for both the every-column and the one-column query. Why is it no help in seeing column pruning?
hint: What does it actually add up?

choices.text: Column pruning did not happen
choices.why: `ReadSchema` shows two columns, and the timings differ by half.

choices.text: It counts files opened, not bytes read
choices.why: Right. The time showed the difference the metric could not.

choices.text: Both queries read the same rows
choices.why: Rows are not the issue; columns are.

choices.text: The metric is only filled for CSV
choices.why: It was filled; it measures something else.

prompt: Why does `pruning.py` build each query afresh before timing it, instead of running the same DataFrame twice?
hint: What would the second run reuse?

choices.text: A DataFrame can only run once
choices.why: It can run any number of times.

choices.text: The first run's shuffle would be reused
choices.why: Right. The second run would time almost nothing.

choices.text: Python caches the answer
choices.why: Python keeps nothing; Spark's shuffle files are the reuse.

choices.text: The files change between runs
choices.why: They do not.

prompt: What does `ReadSchema: struct<kind:string,book_id:int>` on a scan mean?

choices.text: Those two columns are cached
choices.why: Nothing is cached here.

choices.text: The result will have those two columns
choices.why: The result is a single count.

choices.text: The files only contain those two columns
choices.why: They contain seven; the query needs two.

choices.text: Only those two columns will be read
choices.why: Right. The other five are skipped in the files.

prompt: Why does column pruning save little on a CSV file?
hint: How do you find the third field of a line?

choices.text: A line must be read whole to find any field in it
choices.why: Right. It saves parsing, not reading.

choices.text: Spark does not prune columns for CSV at all
choices.why: It prunes what it parses; the bytes still pass.

choices.text: CSV files are always compressed
choices.why: Not always, and compression is not the reason.

choices.text: CSV columns have no names
choices.why: The header gives names; the layout is the problem.

prompt: With the filter `day = '2025-03-14'`, how many files did the scan open?
A query filters `ts` between two times on 14 March, with no filter on `day`. How many directories does it open?

choices.text: None; it fails without a `day` filter
choices.why: It runs, reading everything.

choices.text: One, because the times fall on one day
choices.why: True of the data, unknown to the planner.

choices.text: Two, the day and the next
choices.why: Without a partition filter there is no pruning at all.

choices.text: All 365
choices.why: Right. Filter on `day` as well to prune.

prompt: Match each line of a scan to what it decides.

pairs.right: What the reader may skip inside a file

right_distractors: How many executors run the scan

prompt: Choosing the day through a Python UDF gave the same answer. What did it cost?

choices.text: Nothing; the UDF was pruned like a built-in
choices.why: Its plan has no `PartitionFilters` line.

choices.text: All 365 files were opened, for one day's answer
choices.why: Right. The planner could not turn the UDF into a directory.

choices.text: The answer was approximate
choices.why: It was exactly 1,304, the same.

choices.text: It failed on the days that were not 14 March
choices.why: It returned false for them, after reading them.

prompt: Why can `F.date_format("day", "MM-dd") == "03-14"` prune partitions when the Python UDF cannot?

choices.text: It is cheaper to compute
choices.why: Cost is not the reason; where it can run is.

choices.text: Java evaluates it on each directory's value
choices.why: Right. A Python function would need Python there.

choices.text: It returns a string
choices.why: The return type does not matter.

choices.text: UDFs are banned from filters
choices.why: The UDF filter worked, slowly.

prompt: `kind = 'purchase'` was pushed to the reader, yet the one-day scan handed on all 65,753 rows. Why?
hint: What does the reader use to skip?

choices.text: The filter was applied twice by mistake
choices.why: Applying it again above the scan is by design.

choices.text: No row group could be ruled out
choices.why: Right. Skipping needs grouped values; lesson 10 sorts them.

choices.text: Pushdown only works on numbers
choices.why: Strings have min and max too.

choices.text: The UDF disabled pushdown
choices.why: This query had no UDF.

prompt: What does `AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false` at the top of a plan mean?
hint: Final according to whom, and when?

choices.text: Adaptive execution is turned off
choices.why: The node is only there when it is on.

choices.text: The plan is revised as stages finish
choices.why: Right. After the run it reads `true`.

choices.text: The query has not been optimised yet
choices.why: The logical optimisation is done; AQE adds run-time changes.

choices.text: The plan has an error
choices.why: It is the normal state before running.

prompt: Why did AQE put `AQEShuffleRead coalesced` above the grouping's shuffle?

choices.text: A partition was too large and had to be split
choices.why: That is skew handling, lesson 8; here they were tiny.

choices.text: The join had to become a broadcast
choices.why: It was a broadcast from the start.

choices.text: The executors ran out of memory
choices.why: Nothing failed.

choices.text: Most of the 200 partitions were empty
choices.why: Right. It merged them into a few of sensible size.

prompt: Which of these can adaptive execution not change?

choices.text: Splitting a partition far larger than the rest
choices.why: It can; lesson 8.

choices.text: The number of partitions after a shuffle
choices.why: It coalesces them, as section 10 showed.

choices.text: Which files the first stage reads
choices.why: Right. That is decided before any shuffle has happened.

choices.text: A shuffle join turning into a broadcast join
choices.why: It can, when a side turns out small.

prompt: `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` printed `10485760b`. How many MiB is that?
With the threshold at -1, what replaced the broadcast join?

choices.text: No join; the query failed
choices.why: It planned fine, the other way.

choices.text: A `BroadcastNestedLoopJoin`
choices.why: That is for joins with no equality condition.

choices.text: A broadcast of the clicks instead of the books
choices.why: -1 turns broadcasting off for both sides.

choices.text: A `SortMergeJoin`
choices.why: Right. The reduce-side join of lesson 4.

prompt: The join was estimated at 783.6 GiB. Why was the broadcast choice still right?
hint: Which estimate does a broadcast depend on?

choices.text: Only the small side's estimate mattered
choices.why: Right. 15.5 KiB for the books was close.

choices.text: AQE corrected the estimate before choosing
choices.why: The choice was made before running, from the estimate.

choices.text: The join really produced 783.6 GiB
choices.why: It produced about 22 million rows of a few bytes each.

choices.text: Estimates are ignored for joins
choices.why: They decide the strategy.

prompt: A report reads `data/silver/clicks`, keeps rows where `udf_month(ts) == 12`, and is slow. Which rewrite saves most?

choices.text: Keep the UDF on `ts` and add executors
choices.why: Still every file and every row through Python.

choices.text: Filter `day` on December with built-ins
choices.why: Right. 31 directories opened instead of 365, and no trip to Python.

choices.text: Replace the UDF with `F.month("ts") == 12`
choices.why: Better, but `ts` is not the partition column; every directory is still opened.

choices.text: Read the raw CSV instead
choices.why: Slower in every way.

pairs.right: A small side copied to every task
